searches.note: Thirty nine searches of a share of sixty; twenty one unspent. Five were shared: two on the Rheingau's minimum must weights (the second restricted to Hessian state domains, which reached the Regierungspräsidium Darmstadt's table), one on the Ortsteile, one on Charta's founding and one on Erstes Gewächs. Thirteen were restricted to a house's or a body's own domain (schloss-johannisberg.de five times, weingut-robert-weil.com once, schlossvollrads.com three times, vdp.de once, kloster-eberbach.de twice, the Hessian domains once) and read as primary through their summaries. Two returned nothing on their question (the estate history of Schloss Johannisberg by keyword, and the death of the Breuer son in German). One WebFetch was tried, on the estate's Grünlack sheet at schloss-johannisberg.de, and refused by the network; no other fetch was tried.

method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library, region record and question banks and on the writer's memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and dates, the classifications and their years, the sites and soils, the making, the label words and every beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library, region record and question banks, and two reference books, none opened) is replaced by pages a search returned, read: search; marked primary where the result came from the producer's own domain (schloss-johannisberg.de, weingut-robert-weil.com, schlossvollrads.com, kloster-eberbach.de, Suntory's own brand page), the VDP, the German Wine Institute or a Hessian state office.

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's or critic's own site was read as a lead and never cited. Facts the library states stand as the brief allows, except where a search contested them (the Rotlack as the entry to the colour code, the Vollrads Kabinett labelled by the estate's name alone, Breuer's spontaneous fermentation), reported below.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score (critics' marks and shop prices met in results, none carried), nothing volatile (hectares, bottle sizes and a yearly alcohol kept out of the shipped text), no judging superlative (the lint's notes on lightest and the first step answered with below Spätlese), no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors of one kind and an explanation naming the nearest wrong option. Schema note: the checked blocks carry by: refuter, the only value schema.cjs accepts.

tested: The founding of about 1100: Benedictines under the Archbishop of Mainz, linked to St Alban, by Wikipedia and Wines of Germany; one article gives 1090; the library's 1100 stands as about 1100, and the estate counts twelve centuries of wine on the hill (its history page's own title): confirmed.

Fulda: the Prince-Abbot bought the ruins in June 1716 and made a summer palace, by Wikipedia and Wines of Germany; the Thirty Years War as the cause of the ruin was in no source read: confirmed without the war.
Riesling alone from 1720: the estate's own pages (oldest pure Riesling estate since 1720, a claim of a first kept out of the text) and the library: confirmed.

The legend of 1775: the courier sent to Fulda came back late, eight or fourteen days by different accounts, four weeks in a blog; the grapes overripe and touched by noble rot; the estate's anniversary pages; told as a legend: confirmed, weeks late corrected.
The first Auslese of 1787 and Eiswein of 1858: 1858 on the estate's own timeline; 1787 from one writer's book cited at second hand, 1779 in another account: 1858 kept, 1787 cut.

Metternich: on 1 July 1816 the Emperor Francis I gave the schloss to his foreign minister, by the estate's history page; the tithe to the Habsburgs by Wikipedia and a second page; Metternich 1773 to 1859 and Francis I 1768 to 1835 by Wikipedia and Britannica: confirmed, chancellor corrected to foreign minister.

The capsule code: Rotlack Kabinett, Grünlack Spätlese and Silberlack dry by the estate's own sheets and shop, a merchant and Falstaff; Gelblack the dry estate Riesling below the Rotlack; Orangelack, Bronzelack, Rosalack, Goldlack and Blaulack also met; whether the code dates from 1820 rests on one merchant: confirmed for the three colours the record names.

The Grünlack itself: stainless steel and fine lees to a March bottling, some 76 grams of sugar and 8 to 8.5 per cent, Taunus quartzite under loam and loess with a little iron oxide, by the estate's 2022 and 2023 sheets: making and sites corrected.
The Spätlese floor of 85 degrees Oechsle: the Regierungspräsidium Darmstadt's table for the Rheingau gives 85 for white grapes; Wikipedia gives 85 and one importer 90: confirmed by the primary.

The rules: nobody living named (the estate's managing director appears in results unnamed), no price or score carried, nothing volatile, no superlative (the estate's oldest pure Riesling estate kept out), British, no dash; both questions have one key, options of one kind and an explanation naming the nearest wrong option: sound.

changed.was: The hill at Johannisberg took its first vines from Benedictine monks, who founded a monastery there around 1100. After the Thirty Years War left it ruined, the Prince-Abbots of Fulda took the estate, built the schloss and in 1720 planted the hill to Riesling alone. In 1775, so the story goes, the courier carrying the Prince-Abbot's leave to begin the harvest arrived weeks late; the grapes had shrivelled and rotted on the vine, the wine made from them was a revelation, and Spätlese, the late harvest, entered the language. The estate's chronology adds an Auslese in 1787 and an Eiswein in 1858. In 1816, after the Congress of Vienna, the Emperor Francis I of Austria (1768 to 1835) gave the schloss to his chancellor, Prince Klemens von Metternich (1773 to 1859), on condition that a tenth of each harvest went to the Habsburgs. The estate came to code its wines by the colour of the capsule, the Rotlack for Kabinett, the Grünlack for Spätlese and the Silberlack for its dry Grosses Gewächs, so a guest can read the style from across the room. Pour the Grünlack Spätlese with the legend, and tell it as the estate's claim rather than as proven history.
changed.now: The estate counts twelve centuries of wine on its hill, and around 1100 Benedictine monks founded a monastery there. By 1716, when the Prince-Abbot of Fulda bought it, the monastery lay in ruins; Fulda built a summer palace and from 1720 planted the hill to Riesling alone. In 1775, so the story goes, the courier sent to Fulda for the Prince-Abbot's leave to pick came back late; the grapes had shrivelled and caught noble rot, the wine made from them was a revelation, and Spätlese, the late harvest, entered the language. The estate's chronology adds its first Eiswein in 1858. On 1 July 1816, after the Congress of Vienna, the Emperor Francis I of Austria (1768 to 1835) gave the schloss to his foreign minister, Prince Klemens von Metternich (1773 to 1859), with a tithe of the yield owed each year to the Habsburgs. By its own account its cellar library holds bottles back to 1748. The estate came to code its wines by the colour of the capsule, the Rotlack for Kabinett, the Grünlack for Spätlese and the Silberlack for its dry Grosses Gewächs, so a guest can read the style from across the room. The Grünlack carries the legend into the glass; tell it as the estate's claim rather than as proven history.
changed.why: The estate's history counts twelve centuries of wine and gives 1 July 1816 and the foreign minister; Wikipedia and Wines of Germany give the purchase of the ruins by the Prince-Abbot of Fulda in 1716, the summer palace and the tithe; the courier was eight or fourteen days late by different accounts, not weeks; the Auslese of 1787 is dated 1779 in another account and is cut; the Eiswein of 1858 is on the estate's timeline; the cellar library to 1748 is the estate's; Metternich's and Francis I's dates by Wikipedia and Britannica.

changed.was: The estate began with a scholar. Its founder, a German who taught at the Sorbonne in Paris, left France after the war of 1870 and in 1875 bought his first vineyards at Kiedrich. In 1879 he bought the estate of an English baronet in the village, with its manor house and vines, and made it the family's home. As the house tells it, its sweet wines were poured at the imperial courts of Europe before the First World War, and the Gräfenberg, the steep slope behind the village, became the estate's signature. In 1988 the family sold a majority of the estate to the Japanese house of Suntory, and a great grandson of the founder ran it with the new capital behind him. From the 1990s the estate was known for making the whole botrytis ladder from the Gräfenberg, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein, year after year where others managed them only now and then, while making a dry Grosses Gewächs from the same slope. That steadiness made Weil the usual answer when a question asks for German sweet wine outside the Mosel. Against a Saar Trockenbeerenauslese the Rheingau's way with noble rot is plain to taste: the same grape in a fuller, firmer frame.
changed.now: The estate began with a scholar. Its founder, a German professor at the Sorbonne in Paris, bought his first vines on the Kiedricher Berg in 1867, by the estate's account, and the events before the war of 1870 drove him out of France. In 1875, the year the house counts as its founding, he added more of the Kiedrich slope, and he bought the manor house of a late English baronet in the village, which became the seat of the estate. As the house tells it, its Spätlese and Auslese wines were poured at imperial and royal courts across Europe. In 1988 the Japanese house of Suntory took a majority of the estate, with the founder's great grandson, the fourth generation, in charge of the wine. By the estate's own account the Gräfenberg has given every Prädikat up to Trockenbeerenauslese in every vintage since 1989, while the same slope gives a dry Grosses Gewächs. That run made Weil the usual counterweight to the Mosel when a question asks for German sweet Riesling. Against a Saar Trockenbeerenauslese the Rheingau's way with noble rot is plain to taste: the same grape in a fuller, firmer frame.
changed.why: The estate's own history: first vineyards on the Kiedricher Berg in 1867 while a professor at the Sorbonne, events before the war of 1870/71 forced him to leave, 1875 the expansion, the manor of the late English baronet, the wines at imperial and royal courts; Suntory's own page and two secondary sources for 1988; the estate's own words and a tasting listing for every Prädikat each vintage since 1989; 1879 for the manor is in no source (one gives 1875).

changed.was: A sale of wine recorded in 1211 is where Schloss Vollrads begins its own history, and the estate counts it among the longest unbroken records of wine sales in the world. The moated tower at its heart was built in the fourteenth century by the Greiffenclau family, knights of the Rheingau, who held Vollrads for centuries and added the manor house beside it. The vineyard lies in one piece around the tower, and the label, since the estate is an Ortsteil, names the estate alone, with no village or vineyard before it. In 1984 the head of the family was among the founders of Charta, the growers' association that set out to bring dry Rheingau Riesling back to the table and led, in 1999, to the Erstes Gewächs law of Hesse. After his death in 1997 the family's centuries at Vollrads ended, and the estate passed to new owners who kept its name and its Riesling. The Kabinett is the estate's everyday voice and the clearest sign of its long habit of making one wine in several styles, dry, off dry and fruity. Its label is the lesson, an estate's name standing alone with the style written in a single word.
changed.now: In 1211 the Greiffenclau family appear at Winkel in the service of the Archbishop of Mainz, and a sale of wine recorded that year is where Schloss Vollrads begins its own history. From about 1330 the family lived in the moated tower at the heart of the estate, for more than three hundred and fifty years, until they built the manor house beside it in 1684. The name passed in time to the Matuschka-Greiffenclau line. Erwein Graf Matuschka-Greiffenclau (1938 to 1997), who took over the indebted estate in 1975, was among the founders in 1984 of Charta, the growers' association that set out to bring dry Rheingau Riesling back to the table; its vineyards joined the VDP in 1999, the year the Rheingau's Erstes Gewächs arrived. His death in 1997 ended nearly eight centuries of the family at Vollrads, and the estate passed to a regional savings bank, the Nassauische Sparkasse, which kept its name and its Riesling. The Kabinett is the estate's everyday voice and the plainest sign of its long habit of making one wine in more than one style. Its label is the lesson: read feinherb, or its absence, before you pour.

changed.was: Cistercian monks sent from Clairvaux by Bernard of Clairvaux (1090 to 1153) founded the abbey of Eberbach in a wooded valley above Hattenheim in 1136. They cleared the slope below the forest and laid out the Steinberg in the twelfth century, and over the centuries they closed it with a stone wall, finished, by most accounts, in the eighteenth. The abbey grew into one of the large wine businesses of medieval Germany, sending its wine down the Rhine to the markets of Cologne. In 1712 the monks set aside a cellar, the Cabinet, for their reserve wines, and the word, as Kabinett, later came to name a Prädikat. When church lands were secularised in 1803 the abbey passed to the Duke of Nassau, with Nassau to Prussia in 1866, and after 1945 to the new state of Hesse, whose state wine domaine made the abbey and the Steinberg its home. Because the Steinberg is an Ortsteil, its wine is labelled Steinberger, with no village name, and it has stayed one block for some eight centuries in a country of divided vineyards. One wall, one vineyard, one name: eight centuries of monastic history stand behind the label.
changed.now: An earlier religious house in the wooded valley above Hattenheim had failed when, in 1136, twelve monks came from Clairvaux, the abbey of Bernard of Clairvaux (1090 to 1153), at the request of the Archbishop of Mainz and founded the Cistercian abbey of Eberbach. Their Steinberg, on the slope below the forest, appears by name in the abbey's register of goods in 1211, and in the eighteenth century the monks closed it with a stone wall, finished in 1767. By most accounts the word Cabinet was first written at Eberbach in 1712, for reserve wines the monks set apart in a cellar of their own, and as Kabinett it later came to name a Prädikat. When the abbey was dissolved in 1803 it became the princely wine cellar of the Dukes of Nassau; after Nassau lost the war of 1866 it was a royal Prussian domaine, and after the Second World War it passed to the new state of Hesse, whose state wine domaine made the abbey and the Steinberg its home. The wine law of 1971 registered the Steinberg as a part of Hattenheim, so its wine is labelled Steinberger, with no village name. One wall, one vineyard, one name: eight centuries of monks, dukes, kings and a state stand behind the label.
changed.why: The abbey's own page: twelve monks from Clairvaux at the Archbishop of Mainz's request in 1136, Bernard 1090/91 to 1153; Wikipedia: an earlier house had failed; KuLaDig and an importer: the Steinberg named in the register of 1211; the domaine and Wikipedia: the wall finished in 1767; Wikipedia and a second source: Cabinet first recorded at Eberbach in 1712 for wines set apart in a special cellar; the domaine: 1803 Nassau's princely wine cellar, 1866 Prussia, 1945 or 1946 Hesse; the wine to Cologne was found nowhere; the close no longer calls eight centuries monastic.

picks.ruling: kept: the Grünlack Spätlese carries the estate's legend of 1775 and its colour code, and the plan's note asking for the lack colour and the Prädikat is answered.
kept: the Gräfenberg Trockenbeerenauslese is the wine the estate's own run since 1989 is built on; the dry Grosses Gewächs stands among the others.

kept with a note for the integrator: the Riesling Kabinett holds the plan's words and is the estate's face abroad, but on the estate's own labels since at least 2020 it is printed Winkel Rheingau Riesling Kabinett, a VDP village wine, and the name Schloss Vollrads stands alone on the dry 1716 Cabinet; by rank the dry top wine is the Schlossberg Grosses Gewächs. The record teaches all three.
kept: the Berg Schlossberg is the estate's summit wine by the library and every merchant read.

kept with a note for the integrator: the domaine labels its dry top wine Steinberg Riesling Grosses Gewächs, while Steinberger Riesling trocken sits at the VDP village level; the plan's Steinberger Riesling stands for the historic name of the walled vineyard and the record teaches the difference. A swap of the wine name to the Grosses Gewächs would need the plan's words changed.

codexInTension.says: The red capsule, the entry into the estate's colour code.
codexInTension.against: The estate's Gelblack, its dry estate Riesling, sits below the Rotlack; the Rotlack Kabinett is off dry by the estate's own list.

codexInTension.says: The 1787 Auslese and 1858 Eiswein claims follow the same estate's chronology.
codexInTension.against: The estate's timeline gives the Eiswein of 1858; the Auslese of 1787 was found only at second hand from one writer's book, and another account gives 1779.

codexInTension.says: The estate name stands in place of any vineyard name on the label; the standard example of a property permitted to label by estate.
codexInTension.against: The estate's own sheets print the Kabinett as Winkel Rheingau Riesling Kabinett, a VDP village wine, since at least 2020; the estate's name alone stands on the dry 1716 Cabinet. The why also calls 1211 the oldest documented record of wine sales in Germany, a claim of a first that one source calls weaker; it should be told as the estate's.

codexInTension.says: Kiedricher Grafenberg and Rudesheim without their umlauts; the largest holding in the Grafenberg; Germany's most consistently produced great botrytis Riesling.
